## Research question

The [PhD proposal's RQ1](../../phd/index.qmd) asks *which statistical, econometric and ML
methods most reliably identify market states out of sample*. Reliability, though, is not
self-defining. A method can produce a stable, plausible, well-recovered state estimate that
makes no difference to any decision. So this experiment tests the question underneath:

> **Does conditioning on a market-state estimate improve out-of-sample forecast calibration
> or risk control, *beyond what a continuous volatility signal using the same information
> already provides*?**

That final clause is the entire design. Comparing a state-conditional model against
buy-and-hold, or against nothing, would only demonstrate that volatility is informative —
which nobody disputes. The benchmark here is a model that sees the **same volatility
features and simply does not see the state**. Whatever the state adds over that, and only
that, is the incremental value of state information.

## Hypothesis

From the proposal's own position, and from what this lab has already found in
[regime-conditioning](../regime-conditioning-oos/index.qmd) and
[regime-conditional calibration](../regime-conditional-calibration/index.qmd):

- **H-a.** State information will **not** improve direction forecasts. Expected null.
- **H-b.** State information **will** improve *volatility-regime* calibration.
- **H-c.** A state overlay on volatility targeting will **not** improve risk-adjusted
  outcomes beyond the volatility scaler itself.

H-a and H-c are predictions of failure. Stating them in advance is what makes the result
informative either way.

## Data & method

Daily Nasdaq-100. Eight state estimators — three transparent baselines (moving-average
crossover, trailing-return sign, EWMA slope), a Kalman local-linear-trend filter, a Gaussian
HMM, a Markov-switching regression, and CUSUM and BOCPD change-point detectors — each
producing a **filtered** probability vector over {down, range, up}. Every estimate is causal:
the value at time *t* uses only data up to *t*, enforced by an automated look-ahead test
rather than by inspection. The harness's ninth estimator, a do-nothing constant, is excluded:
a state that never changes carries no information to test, and scoring it would only pad the
comparison count and loosen the deflated bar.

**Every method is scored on identical dates.** Methods that fit parameters surrender a
training window, so their usable spans are shorter than the baselines'. Scoring each against
its own benchmark makes every *individual* comparison fair, but it makes the *ranking* partly
a comparison of periods. So the panel is aligned to the intersection of all eight spans —
**2018-02-06 to 2026-06-26**, 2,108 shared dates, 1,755 scored after the purged walk-forward.
That alignment turned out to matter more than expected; see [what changed](#what-changed-when-the-window-was-aligned).

**Calibration.** Walk-forward logistic regression, purged by the label horizon, comparing
`[rv20, rv60]` against `[rv20, rv60, p_down, p_range, p_up]` on three five-day-ahead targets:
*direction* (return positive), *loss* (return below minus one trailing standard deviation),
and *volatility* (realised volatility above its trailing median). Scored by Brier; a negative
delta means the state helped.

**Significance.** Diebold-Mariano tests on the per-observation loss differential with
Newey-West standard errors, because overlapping five-day labels make the differentials
serially correlated and an i.i.d. error would manufacture significance. With 24 comparisons
the relevant bar is not 1.96: under the null the largest of *N* t-statistics is around
$\sqrt{2\ln N}$, so the [deflated](../backtest-overfitting/index.qmd) threshold is
**|t| > 2.52**. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR is reported alongside.

**Risk control.** Volatility targeting at 10% annualised, with and without a state overlay
that multiplies exposure by $(1 - p_{\text{down}})$ — pre-committed, and purely defensive so
that it can only ever *reduce* exposure. Net of 2bp costs on turnover.

Negative is better; the dashed lines are the deflated bar of |t| > 2.52 for 24 comparisons, and the shaded band between them is the region where nothing can be claimed. Only two bars reach the "helps" side, both on the volatility target; **none** reaches "harms". ## Results

**Direction: a unanimous null.** All eight estimators made direction forecasts *worse* than
the volatility-only benchmark — Brier deltas from +0.0010 to +0.0050 on a baseline of 0.2423,
a base rate of 0.598. But none of those harms is significant: the largest is `bocpd` at
t = +2.25, inside the bar. The honest statement is that state information adds **nothing** to
return timing, not that it actively destroys it.

**Loss: also nothing.** Three of eight are mildly negative and five mildly positive, and no
comparison approaches the bar (largest |t| = 2.21). On a base rate of 0.130 and a baseline
Brier of 0.1134, the state is simply irrelevant to whether next week holds a bad day.

**Volatility regime: one survivor.** `ewma_slope` improves the Brier score by −0.0213
(t = −3.93, FDR p = 0.0020) against a 0.2319 baseline — a **9.2% relative improvement**, and
the only result that clears both the deflated bar and FDR. `return_sign` clears the deflated
bar (−0.0111, t = −2.54) but **fails** FDR at p = 0.117, so it should be read as suggestive
at best. Everything else is inside the band.

**Zero of the twenty-four comparisons is a significant harm.**

**Risk control: the null holds, and the naive reading is a trap.** Against a single
volatility-target baseline — Sharpe 0.830 at 11.1% volatility, −16.7% maximum drawdown,
drawdown/vol −1.502, 6.0× annual turnover:

| measure | how many of the 8 overlays improve on the baseline |
|---|---|
| raw maximum drawdown | **8 of 8** |
| Sharpe ratio | 1 of 8 |
| drawdown per unit of volatility | 3 of 8 |

Read raw drawdown alone and every single overlay "works". That is an artefact: the overlay can
only cut exposure, so it always ends up holding less, and a rule that holds less always shows a
shallower drawdown. Read risk-adjusted and the effect disappears. The one overlay with a higher
Sharpe (`ms_regression`, 0.869) pays for it with 11.2× annual turnover against the baseline's
6.0×.

## What changed when the window was aligned

The first version of this experiment scored each estimator on its own usable span — 2,355 days
for the baselines and BOCPD, 1,755 for the four fitted methods — each against a benchmark run
over the same dates. Every individual comparison was fair. The *ranking* was not, because four
methods were being judged on a period the other four never saw: 2015 to early 2018, which
contains the 2015–16 selloff and Volmageddon.

Aligning everything to the common window changed the conclusions materially:

| result | own-span version | common window |
|---|---|---|
| significant harms | **4 of 24** | **0 of 24** |
| `bocpd` / volatility | −0.0074 (t −2.60), survived | −0.0021 (t −0.43), gone |
| `ewma_slope` / volatility | −0.0171 (t −3.98) | −0.0213 (t −3.93), **stronger** |
| `return_sign` / volatility | −0.0054 (t −1.82) | −0.0111 (t −2.54) |

The four "significant harms" — `bocpd` and `return_sign` on direction and loss, at
t = +3.20 to +4.57 — were **entirely a property of 2015–2018**. They vanish on the common
window. I published that claim, and it was wrong: not wrong arithmetic, but a real effect
attributed to the wrong cause.

`bocpd`'s apparent calibration gain went the same way. It had already decayed on a widening
cross-asset panel (−0.0074 → −0.0047 → −0.0020); the common window independently kills it.
Two unrelated robustness checks agreeing is about as clear as this gets.

`ewma_slope` did the opposite. Its gain **grew** when the easier early period was removed,
which is what a real effect looks like.

## The verdict — and what it means for the proposal

**H-a confirmed.** State does not time returns. Unanimous across eight methods, and now
unanimous without the overstatement: it fails to help rather than measurably hurting.

**H-b confirmed, narrowly.** Exactly one estimator shows a volatility-calibration gain that
survives correction for multiple testing. Seven do not.

**H-c confirmed.** The state overlay adds no risk-adjusted value beyond the volatility scaler.
The same de-risking is available for nothing by simply lowering the volatility target — no
model, no turnover.

This tightens the proposal's central position. "Market-state information is a calibration and
risk-control signal, not a return-timing signal" survives, with two amendments: the calibration
benefit is **specific and rare** rather than general, and the risk-control half does **not**
hold once exposure is properly controlled for.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The awkward result.** The one estimator whose benefit survives correction is `ewma_slope` —
a simple exponentially-weighted trend rule that ranks *worst* on persistence, changing state
every ~5 days. It is a poor state estimator by every stability measure in the harness and the
best one by this decision-value measure. Any account of RQ1 has to explain that rather than
average it away.
:::

I tested the obvious explanation — that a rapidly oscillating state is just re-encoding
volatility through its own instability — by adding the estimator's own causal rolling flip
rate to the **baseline**, so the benchmark already sees the churn. The gain did not collapse.
The confound is ruled out and the mechanism remains unexplained, which is the honest place to
leave it.

## Limitations

- **Single asset.** These twenty-four comparisons are Nasdaq-100 only. On a seven-asset panel
  the `ewma_slope` volatility gain replicated (mean −0.0138). The full-panel deflation, where
  the bar rises to |t| > 3.24 for 189 comparisons, is the outstanding test.
- **A shorter sample.** Aligning the window costs 600 days and removes 2015–2018 entirely. The
  comparison is now like-for-like but rests on a single market era, and one that contains only
  one true crisis.
- **The DM test is slightly liberal.** Its empirical size measured ~0.07 against a nominal
  0.05, so borderline results — `return_sign` especially — deserve more scepticism than their
  p-values suggest.
- **One overlay rule.** $(1 - p_{\text{down}})$ is defensible and pre-committed but arbitrary;
  a different mapping from state to exposure could behave differently.
- **Index, not total return, and no borrowing constraint** on the leveraged volatility target.

## What I learned

Twice now this experiment has taught the same lesson in different clothes: **fix the comparison
before reading the number.** First it was raw drawdown, which made every overlay look
successful until exposure was controlled for. Then it was the scored window, where eight
methods being individually fairly benchmarked still produced an unfair ranking, because four of
them were judged on a harder period than the others.

Neither was a coding error. Both were comparisons that looked obviously fair and were not, and
in both cases the correct comparison reversed the finding. That is the failure mode worth
guarding against — not arithmetic, but a benchmark that quietly answers a different question.

The second lesson is how much a fair benchmark costs a hypothesis. Against buy-and-hold, almost
everything here would have looked like a win. Against a volatility-only model with the same
information, twenty-three of twenty-four comparisons are indistinguishable from noise. That is
the difference between a result and an artefact, and it is the standard the
[LLM-trading literature](../../phd/literature/li-2025-finsaber-llm-evaluation/index.qmd)
conspicuously fails to meet.
